idiom_name: extension for a computed property/method plus an associated object (or ObjectIdentifier table) for stored state
implementation_notes: An extension is Swift's own way of attaching members to a type you do not own: it adds methods, computed properties, initialisers, nested types and protocol conformances to classes, structs and enums, so the capability interface is a protocol the extension makes the subject conform to and the capability query is a cast or an is/as? check. Storage is the part extensions cannot provide - the language guide states that 'extensions can add new computed properties, but they can't add stored properties' - so attached state goes either into a table keyed by ObjectIdentifier (a plain Dictionary or an NSMapTable on Apple platforms) or, for any Objective-C class, into an associated reference created with objc_setAssociatedObject and read with objc_getAssociatedObject. Apple's documentation describes associated references as simulating 'the addition of object instance variables to an existing class' without modifying the class declaration. Prefer a protocol plus composition when the call sites can be changed: associated objects are runtime magic with no compile-time check.
pitfalls: Associated objects exist only for classes reachable through the Objective-C runtime: they are unavailable to Swift structs, enums and non-@objc classes, the key must be a stable unique address (a file-private static var, not a string literal that another extension can reuse), and they are released only when the host object deallocates, so a cycle through the associated object leaks silently.

Retroactive conformance is fragile: conformance cannot be added to a non-final class in a way subclasses inherit predictably, an extension cannot be overridden, and two modules declaring the same conformance for the same type produce a compile-time conflict ('redundant conformance') that is only visible when both modules are linked.

Extension members are resolved statically, so a method later added to the type itself shadows the extension's member; and because extensions cannot declare deinit, an extension that needs cleanup on subject death must register for the subject's lifecycle explicitly.
